source_read: PDF, Experimental and Clinical Psychopharmacology 2: 244-268 (scanned, OCR text layer): text pp. 244-265 read in full (references pp. 265-268 not read); Tables 2-5 and the Results text of pp. 251 and 253 checked against rendered page images (pp. 251, 252, 253, 256, 257, 259).

key_findings.correction: Diagnostic Assessment of Alcohol and Other Drug Dependence, 1st-4th paragraphs (pp. 247-248): the computer scoring is in the 1st paragraph (p. 247), the DSM-III-R criteria in the 2nd, the identical questions in the 3rd and the several-occasions rule in the 4th, which continues on p. 248.
key_findings.note: Content confirmed. The 4th paragraph also says that even as few as six occasions might suffice for dependence, the only hint of the threshold.
All values checked on the page image of p. 251; the printed ratios equal dependence prevalence divided by use prevalence within rounding for every row.
Checked on the page image of p. 256; the oldest band is printed '45+'.
Checked on the page image of p. 259. The text (pp. 255 and 257) names six classes as similar by sex, then alcohol, cannabis and the anxiolytic group; stimulants are the one class never mentioned.

key_findings.correction: The p. 265 sentence is hedged: the authors write that many people who use drugs, perhaps a vast majority, 'do not seem to make a transition to drug dependence'. The card drops 'seem' here and in the interpretation-gap text (claimed).

key_findings.note: The same paragraph calls the ECA cannabis figure a 'disorder' rate, and the next notes that the DSM-III criteria used in the ECA did not provide for cocaine dependence (p. 258). The ECA 1.7% is therefore a DSM-III disorder estimate against an NCS DSM-III-R dependence estimate; the replication timeline should say the match is across diagnostic systems.

reporting_issues.note: Table 4 (p. 257): heroin use 2.7% and 0.7%, dependence 0.8% and 0.1%.
Location detail: the anxiolytic sex difference begins on p. 255 and its figures (6.6% and 12.3%) are on p. 257.
See key finding 2: p. 248 mentions six occasions only as an example.

Table 4's footnote is printed on p. 257 (Table 4 continued), so pp. 251, 256-257 and 259. The footnote of Tables 4 and 5 also sends readers to the 'Assessment of Alcohol and Other Drug Use' section, whereas the tobacco method is under 'Assessment of Tobacco Use and Dependence' (p. 248).

risk_of_bias.note: Overall low (editors' summary) agreed, and JBI fits a prevalence survey. The card rightly separates risk of bias from directness: the limits that matter (snapshot ratio rather than risk, stimulant class rather than methamphetamine, household frame) are about what the figures mean, not about bias in measuring them.

risk_of_bias_domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
risk_of_bias_domains.note: For the stimulant proportion alone the measurement is identical to the other drug classes; the partial-yes concerns comparisons with tobacco.

risk_of_bias_domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed

interpretation_gap.note: Minor agreed. The authors themselves define the ratio as the lifetime prevalence of dependence among people who have used (p. 248, Analysis Procedures), which supports 'minor'; the main invitation to read it as risk is the Results wording that 11.2% 'had progressed to develop dependence' (p. 255).

missed: Text-table mismatches in the odds ratios, checked on the page images: the p. 251 text gives OR 0.59 for tobacco dependence among African Americans, but Table 3 (p. 252) prints 0.45 (0.59 is the Hispanic value); the p. 253 text gives OR 0.87 for tobacco dependence among people living with a spouse, but Table 3 prints 1.05 (0.87 is 'live with other'); and p. 253 gives OR 1.43 for incomes of $20,000-34,000, Table 3 1.44. None concerns stimulants, but they belong with the card's other reporting issues.

Heroin aged 45-54 (pp. 261-262): the text says there were too few people of that age who had used heroin (13 in the sample) to estimate dependence among them, yet Table 4 (p. 257) prints 10.7% (SE 7.7) for that cell.

Card wording (analysis, covariates): three multivariable checks are described without data, not two: race with employment and socio-economic status (pp. 251-253), unemployment (p. 253), and education 'with or without statistical adjustment' (p. 253).
